questions.q: Why did the term DevOps emerge around 2009?
options: To give development teams a new programming language
As a response to the wall between Dev teams (measured on speed) and Ops teams (measured on stability)
Because cloud computing required a new job title
To replace the need for testing entirely
questions.explain: DevOps emerged as a response to the conflicting incentives between Dev (ship fast) and Ops (keep stable), proposing shared ownership instead of a wall between the two.

questions.q: Which three layers make up DevOps?
options: Culture, practices, and tools
Servers, networks, and databases
Planning, coding, and testing only
Managers, developers, and customers
questions.explain: DevOps is commonly described as culture (shared ownership), practices (like CI/CD and infrastructure as code), and tools (like GitHub Actions or Kubernetes) working together.

questions.q: A company buys every popular DevOps tool but keeps a weeks-long manual change-approval process. What's the most accurate assessment?
options: They have fully adopted DevOps because they own the right tools
They have bought software, not adopted DevOps, since culture and practices haven't changed
This is impossible — tools automatically change culture
DevOps requires no process changes at all
questions.explain: Tools alone don't produce DevOps outcomes. Without the cultural and process changes (like faster, trust-based approvals), buying tools doesn't change how the organization actually works.

questions.q: What is the relationship between DevOps and CI/CD?
options: They are exactly the same thing
CI/CD is one important DevOps practice, but DevOps also covers things like infrastructure as code, monitoring, and team structure
CI/CD is a replacement for DevOps
DevOps is a subset of CI/CD
questions.explain: CI/CD is one of DevOps's practices — an important one, and this course's subject — but DevOps is broader, including culture, infrastructure as code, monitoring, and incident response.

questions.q: Why is hiring a single 'DevOps engineer' to handle all deployments considered a common misconception in practice?
options: Because no one should ever have that job title
Because it risks recreating the same silo and wall that DevOps was meant to eliminate
Because DevOps engineers don't need technical skills
Because only Ops teams are allowed to deploy code
questions.explain: If one person or team becomes the sole gatekeeper for deployments, it can recreate the same Dev-vs-Ops wall, even though the job title itself remains useful shorthand for specialized skills.
